nodes.name: Yareta
nodes.desc: A dense, cushion-forming evergreen of the high Andes that grows only a centimetre or so a year. Local people burn it for fuel, which is hard for it to withstand.

nodes.name: Puna bunchgrasses
nodes.desc: Clump-forming grasses such as Festuca and Stipa dominate the puna grasslands. They are the main food of the camelids on the plains.

nodes.name: Pink lagoon algae
nodes.desc: Salt-loving algae that tint Laguna Colorada pink to red. They feed the plankton that the flamingos filter from the water.

nodes.name: Diatoms
nodes.desc: Microscopic glass-walled algae that live on the lake bottom and in the water. Andean and James's flamingos feed mainly on them.

nodes.name: Highland tuco-tuco
nodes.desc: A burrowing rodent of the puna, regularly recorded in the area. It eats roots and plants; the link to its predators is general ecology.

nodes.name: Llama
nodes.desc: Herded by local communities for wool and meat. Grazing by llamas and alpacas is a conservation concern in the reserve.

nodes.name: Vicuña
nodes.desc: Wild camelid that grazes low clump grasses on open plains and rests on the slopes at night. Pumas and culpeos prey on it.

nodes.name: Southern viscacha
nodes.desc: A rock-dwelling rodent that eats mostly grasses and moss and stays close to rocky shelter. The most recorded wild rodent here.

nodes.name: Andean goose
nodes.desc: A large goose of high grassland, bogs and lake shores, living almost entirely above 3,000 m. It eats mostly grasses.

nodes.name: Brine shrimp
nodes.desc: Small crustaceans of salty lakes that filter algae from the water. A flamingo and avocet food source; the exact species here is not confirmed.

nodes.name: Andean flamingo
nodes.desc: Filter feeder with a very broad diet, mostly diatoms from the lake bottom in shallow salty water. Breeds in colonies in the high Andes.

nodes.name: James's flamingo
nodes.desc: Feeds mainly on diatoms and other microscopic algae filtered from the water. Especially abundant at Laguna Colorada.

nodes.name: Chilean flamingo
nodes.desc: Filters algae, plankton, crustaceans and other small invertebrates from shallow lakes and lagoons.

nodes.name: Culpeo (Andean fox)
nodes.desc: An opportunistic fox that eats rodents, hares, birds and carrion, and sometimes young camelids and flamingos. Livestock owners often blame it.

nodes.name: Andean condor
nodes.desc: A huge scavenger that lives in the puna and feeds on carcasses. The Wikipedia puna page lists it among the ecoregion birds.

nodes.name: Andean avocet
nodes.desc: A wader of high salt lakes that sweeps its upturned bill through shallow water for small invertebrates. Well recorded in the area.

nodes.name: Puma
nodes.desc: The top predator of the puna. Hunts vicuñas and other camelids and also takes viscachas, and may kill culpeos.

nodes.name: Intense sunlight
nodes.desc: Thin air at 4,200 to 5,400 m means strong sun for the algae, grasses and cushion plants.

nodes.name: Scarce rain and snowmelt
nodes.desc: The puna is dry. Meltwater and rare rain feed the grasslands, bogs and lagoons.

nodes.name: Salt-lake water
nodes.desc: Shallow, salty, mineral-rich lagoons with borates and sulfates set the home of the algae, diatoms and brine shrimp.

nodes.name: Sparse stony soil
nodes.desc: Sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor ground that yareta prefers and the grasses must make do with.

nodes.name: Soil microbes
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses slowly in the cold, dry air, returning nutrients to the soil.
